title: Choosing the right crochet hook size
subtitle: Match the hook to the yarn weight, then adjust for the fabric you want
excerpt: Hook size matches yarn weight. The yarn label suggests a hook range; the pattern names a specific hook; your tension tells you whether to step up or down within the range. The match controls the size and the drape of the finished fabric.
sourceNotes: Modern Craft Yarn Council standard hook-size recommendations. UK / US / Japanese hook conversion data drawn from manufacturer references (Pony, Clover, Tulip).

glossaryTerms.definition: The translation between metric (4 mm), US lettered (G/6), and Japanese sizes. The same physical hook is named differently in different conventions. The CrochetHook table on every pattern page surfaces all three.

heroPrompt: A row of crochet hooks of different sizes laid out from smallest (1.5 mm) to largest (10 mm) on a pale background, with a small swatch of cream DK cotton in the middle showing a 4 mm hook in use.

content.text: Hook size matches yarn weight. Yarn labels print a recommended hook range; patterns name a specific hook within that range. Your tension determines whether to step up or down within the range. The match controls the size of the finished piece and the drape of the fabric.
DK — 4 to 4.5 mm. The British default is 4 mm.
A smaller hook within the range gives tighter, denser fabric with more stitches per 10 cm. Used for structure-heavy pieces — bags, baskets, amigurumi, dishcloths that need to hold their shape.
A larger hook within the range gives looser, drapier fabric with fewer stitches per 10 cm. Used for blankets, shawls, garments where drape matters more than structure.
When two ends of the range produce very different fabrics from the same yarn, both are correct — they're different design choices. Pick the hook to match the fabric you want.

If your hands work the pattern's named hook too tight, go UP a size. If your hands work it too loose, go DOWN a size. The pattern's hook is the designer's recommendation; your hook is the one that produces the designer's gauge with your hands.

Half-sizes matter. 4.5 mm is between 4 mm and 5 mm; sometimes the right hook for a DK cotton is the 4.5 mm even when the yarn label says 4 mm. The swatch tells you. Quarter-sizes (3.75 mm, 4.25 mm) exist but most beginners can get away with full and half sizes.
British patterns use metric mm. American patterns use letter codes (B/1, C/2, D/3, ... J/10, K/10.5). Japanese patterns use Japanese-specific sizes.
between the three is not always one-to-one; the same physical hook may be labelled slightly differently by different manufacturers.

Metal hooks (aluminium, steel) slide easily through stitches and are the default for most modern crochet. Wooden and bamboo hooks have more grip on slippery yarn — useful for cotton and silk. Plastic hooks are lightweight and warm to the hand, common in cheaper beginner sets.

Handle shape matters more than material. A shaped handle (ergonomic, with a flat thumb-rest) reduces hand fatigue across long projects. A round-shaft hook (no handle) is faster for experienced crocheters but harder on the joints. For first hooks, ergonomic handles are worth the extra cost.

Once a hook range is familiar for a yarn weight, the swatch confirms the choice. The reading on gauge swatching basics walks through the swatch in detail. For hand strain across long sessions, the reading on hook hold and ergonomics covers grip styles and rest breaks.
